row.basis: built city joined together
row.note: The commentary says parts are joined into a firm whole; Psalm 122 calls Jerusalem a city built and compactly joined together, giving that construction image a communal form.

row.basis: joined wall; people minded to work
row.note: The commentary makes work lay bricks and counsel join pieces; Nehemiah says the wall was joined together while the whole people had a mind to work, uniting labor and assembly in one scene.

row.basis: frame tenons received by silver sockets
row.note: The commentary’s door foot fitting its socket has a precise joinery counterpart in the tabernacle frames, whose tenons sit over paired silver sockets; the image is exact fitting rather than a loose attachment.

row.basis: curtains clasped into one tabernacle
row.note: The commentary glosses counsel as connecting one thing to another; Exodus describes woven curtains fastened by clasps so they become one tabernacle, making joining a concrete act of assembly.

row.basis: bones came together bone to bone
row.note: The commentary calls the meeting place of bones haqq; in Ezekiel’s vision the dry bones come together bone to bone before sinews and flesh return, turning that junction into the first step of bodily restoration.

row.basis: body held together by joints; each part works
row.note: The commentary joins work, repair, and fitted parts in one structure; Ephesians describes a body joined through its joints, with each part working as it should so the whole builds itself up.

row.basis: speak truth to neighbor; members of one another
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel connect people; Ephesians tells each person to speak truth with a neighbor because they are members of one another, joining truthful speech to communal interdependence.

row.basis: speak truth each to neighbor
row.note: The commentary’s repeated mutual counsel in truth is directly echoed by Zechariah’s instruction to speak truth to one another and judge truthfully for peace in the gates.

row.basis: does righteousness and speaks truth in the heart
row.note: The commentary places righteous action beside truthful counsel; Psalm 15 describes the person who does righteousness and speaks truth inwardly, joining ethical conduct and truth in one portrait.

row.basis: truthful lips endure; lying tongue is momentary
row.note: The commentary calls haqq a weighty, sound word; Proverbs says truthful lips stand forever while a lying tongue lasts only a moment, making durability an effect of truthful speech.

row.basis: threefold cord not quickly broken
row.note: The commentary develops tightly woven thread and pieces made secure by joining; Ecclesiastes says a threefold cord is not quickly snapped, a direct image of strength through strands joined together.

row.basis: stir one another to love and good works
row.note: The commentary’s mutual counsel connects people in constructive action; Hebrews asks readers to consider one another and stir each other toward love and good works, making that reciprocity explicitly ethical.

row.basis: encourage and build one another up
row.note: The commentary says counsel joins parts into a sound structure; Paul tells the community both to encourage one another and to build one another up, transferring the construction image to mutual support.

row.basis: love in deed and truth
row.note: The commentary puts work and haqq together in a constructive account; 1 John says love must be shown in deed and truth, pairing action with truth while warning against speech alone.

row.basis: house on rock; hears and does the words
row.note: The commentary sets sound construction against a weak house; Jesus’ wise builder hears and does his words and builds on rock, making practiced teaching the secure foundation.

row.basis: neighbors help and urge one another
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel connect and strengthen parts; Isaiah depicts people helping a neighbor and telling a brother to be strong, a concrete scene of reciprocal strengthening.

row.basis: spider’s house as failed confidence
row.note: The commentary names the spider’s house as the opposite of what is sound and well-fitted; Job compares a godless person’s confidence to a spider’s house, explicitly making that dwelling an image of unreliable refuge.

row.basis: spider webs cannot serve as clothing or cover
row.note: The commentary contrasts firm weaving with the spider’s insubstantial house; Isaiah says the webs woven by wrongdoers cannot become garments or cover them, giving the web a specific failure as protective fabric.

row.basis: justice as line; righteousness as plumb line
row.note: The commentary’s fitting door and sound construction make correctness spatially exact; Isaiah measures with justice and righteousness and says hail sweeps away a refuge of lies, connecting moral truth, proper alignment, and a failed shelter.

row.basis: house built by wisdom and established by understanding
row.note: The commentary’s builder’s work produces a structure made sound; Proverbs says wisdom builds a house and understanding establishes it, an explicit pairing of construction with stability.

row.basis: one lifts the companion who falls
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel connect separate parts; Ecclesiastes says one companion can lift the other after a fall, giving that connection a practical form of repair and support.

row.basis: reprove neighbor rather than bear sin
row.note: The commentary’s repeated counsel concerns people correcting and joining one another; Leviticus commands frank reproof of a neighbor to prevent sin, a specific ethical form of corrective counsel.

row.basis: exhort one another daily against deception
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel part of a sound communal structure; Hebrews calls for daily mutual exhortation so no one is hardened by sin’s deceit, showing counsel as protection against moral failure.

row.basis: pursue peace and mutual upbuilding
row.note: The commentary’s joining image treats connection as constructive; Paul tells the community to pursue peace and what builds one another up, making the goal of connection communal edification.

row.basis: house built by injustice and unpaid labor
row.note: The commentary’s work and repair make a sound structure; Jeremiah condemns a ruler who builds his house through unrighteousness and unpaid labor, exposing a building that embodies injustice rather than repair.

row.basis: baked bricks and bitumen mortar
row.note: The commentary says the builder uses mudbrick; the Babel builders make fired bricks and use bitumen for mortar, a concrete ancient building parallel whose surrounding story gives collective construction a different aim.

row.basis: building to make a name and avoid scattering
row.note: The commentary’s joined parts belong to a constructive moral community; Babel’s builders seek a name for themselves and fear being scattered, making their unity an ambitious self-protective project rather than the commentary’s ethical repair.

row.basis: the builders are scattered
row.note: The commentary presents joining as a way to repair and secure; after Babel’s construction, God scatters the builders, a reversal in which a project meant to hold people together ends in dispersal.

row.basis: wall coated over a claim of peace
row.note: The commentary calls speech sound when it is firmly founded; Ezekiel condemns prophets who say “peace” when there is no peace while people build a wall and coat it with whitewash, joining false speech to a deceptive structure.

row.basis: whitewashed wall falls in storm
row.note: The commentary contrasts secure construction with a weak house; Ezekiel predicts that the whitewashed wall will fall under flooding rain and hail, exposing a façade that cannot hold.

row.basis: spider webs woven by wrongdoers
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes firm weaving with the spider’s weak dwelling; Isaiah says wrongdoers weave spider webs, linking the spider image to destructive rather than protective work.

row.basis: house built on sand
row.note: The commentary contrasts firm, fitted construction with a fragile shelter; Jesus’ foolish builder puts his house on sand, specifying the unstable foundation behind failure.

row.basis: house collapses with a great fall
row.note: The commentary contrasts a sound structure with a weak house; Jesus says the sand-built house falls when storm waters and winds strike, making collapse the consequence of a bad foundation.

row.basis: builder lays a foundation and must take care how he builds
row.note: The commentary makes construction an image for coordinated action; Paul describes himself as a skilled builder who laid a foundation and warns each builder to take care, making workmanship and responsibility explicit.

row.basis: gold, stone, wood, hay, straw as building materials
row.note: The commentary distinguishes sound construction from the spider’s weak house; Paul lists materials of sharply different durability for what people build, making the quality of the work consequential.

row.basis: each person’s work is tested by fire
row.note: The commentary links work to a structure that can hold or fail; Paul says fire will disclose and test each builder’s work, adding an explicit test of what construction can endure.

row.basis: living stones built into a spiritual house
row.note: The commentary turns building and joined pieces into a moral image; 1 Peter calls its readers living stones being built into a spiritual house, giving communal construction a religious interpretation.

row.basis: hears words but does not do them
row.note: The commentary contrasts constructive deeds with a weak house; Jesus’ foolish builder hears but does not do the words, and so builds on sand, making the missing practice the moral fault behind the unstable structure.

row.basis: עָמָל ~ ع م ل; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: Psalm 127 says that without YHWH building the house, its builders עָמָלוּ, “toil,” in vain; this matches the commentary’s builder using brick through a possible root correspondence while stressing that labor alone can be futile.

row.basis: חָקַק ~ ح ق ق; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: Job asks that his words be written and inscribed in a book; the commentary calls haqq a solid, weighty word, so this possible root correspondence connects speech with durable inscription without proving cognacy.

row.basis: צָלַח ~ ص ل ح; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: The righteous person in Psalm 1 is like a fruitful tree and whatever he does succeeds; this possible root correspondence adds the outcome of righteous action, while Hebrew צלח means prosper or advance rather than the commentary’s repairing or righteous deed.

row.basis: עָמָל ~ ع م ل; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: Ecclesiastes calls the toil and work of the speaker’s hands vanity; this possible root correspondence shares the commentary’s labor field but gives toil a weary, futile evaluation unlike the constructive brick-laying image.

row.basis: צָלַח ~ ص ل ح; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: Deuteronomy says the cursed person will not צלח, “succeed,” in his ways; this is only a possible root link, but its failure amid oppression offers a contrast to the commentary’s righteous work as constructive action.

row.basis: bones woven in secret
row.note: The commentary joins firm weaving with the meeting of bones; Psalm 139 says the speaker’s bones were not hidden while he was intricately woven, bringing both bodily structure and weaving into one image.

row.basis: bones and sinews knit into a body
row.note: The commentary treats the meeting of bones as a fitted joint; Job describes God clothing the speaker with skin and flesh and knitting him together with bones and sinews, a distinct image of bodily assembly.

row.basis: bone of my bones
row.note: The commentary names the meeting of bones as haqq; the first human recognizes the woman as bone of his bones, making shared bodily substance a kinship image rather than an anatomical junction.

row.basis: cling and become one flesh
row.note: The commentary says pieces are joined into a sound whole; Genesis describes two people clinging and becoming one flesh, a relational form of joining that adds kinship to the construction image.

row.basis: repairer of the breach
row.note: The commentary defines repair as the opposite of corruption; Isaiah calls the restored people repairers of a breach and restorers of streets, making repair both structural and communal.

row.basis: heals broken hearts and binds wounds
row.note: The commentary’s salih repairs what is spoiled; the Psalm depicts God healing broken hearts and binding wounds, applying repair directly to damaged persons.

row.basis: heals after tearing and binds after striking
row.note: The commentary opposes repair to corruption; Hosea calls the people to return because the one who tore them will heal them and bind their wounds, making restoration follow damage.

row.basis: potter reshapes a marred vessel
row.note: The commentary says the good work repairs what is spoiled; Jeremiah’s potter reworks a marred vessel into another form, a concrete image of repair through reshaping.

row.basis: one person sharpens another
row.note: The commentary makes mutual counsel join and strengthen separate parts; Proverbs says one person sharpens another as iron sharpens iron, a direct image of reciprocal strengthening.

row.basis: hearts knit together in love
row.note: The commentary says mutual advice connects pieces and haqq makes the weave firm; Colossians speaks of hearts knit together in love and reaching full assurance, linking cohesion with shared understanding.

row.basis: whole structure joined and growing into a temple
row.note: The commentary fits parts into a secure structure; Ephesians describes the whole building being joined together and growing into a holy temple, an architectural image for a community.

row.basis: stones fitted into the tower
row.note: The commentary says one piece is joined to another; in the Shepherd’s vision, stones fit together in the tower identified with the Church, giving that connection an early Christian communal interpretation.

row.basis: tested stone and firm foundation
row.note: The commentary stresses soundness and exact fit; Isaiah describes a tested cornerstone laid as a firm foundation, connecting reliable construction with trust.

row.basis: rejected stone becomes the cornerstone
row.note: The commentary’s fitted door and joined structure depend on a sound meeting point; the Psalm’s rejected stone becomes the head of the corner, making a once-discarded piece structurally decisive.

row.basis: rejected stone as cornerstone
row.note: Jesus applies the rejected-stone saying to the builders’ judgment of him; this Christian reading of Psalm 118 makes the building image a reversal in which the rejected one becomes structurally central.

row.basis: Isaiah’s chosen cornerstone applied to Christ
row.note: The commentary’s firm fit and foundation imagery meets Peter’s citation of Isaiah’s tested cornerstone as Christ, adding a Christian interpretation in which trust in the chosen stone prevents shame.

row.basis: faith without works is dead
row.note: The commentary makes work place bricks and repair what is broken; James insists that faith without works is dead, directly pairing belief with enacted conduct while adding a distinct argument about their necessity.

row.basis: wise woman builds; folly tears down
row.note: The commentary’s good work repairs and constructs; Proverbs contrasts a wise woman building her house with folly tearing it down, making the same household image express constructive and destructive conduct.

row.basis: divided house cannot stand
row.note: The commentary makes counsel join parts into a stable structure; Jesus says a house divided against itself cannot stand, giving disunity the opposite structural consequence.

row.basis: cultivated vineyard yields wild grapes
row.note: The commentary’s builder and repairer produce a sound moral structure; Isaiah’s owner clears stones, plants a vineyard, and builds its tower, yet receives wild grapes, a crafted project whose result fails its purpose.

row.basis: justice expected but bloodshed found
row.note: The commentary joins constructive action with haqq; Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and says God expected justice and righteousness but found bloodshed and a cry, making failed ethical fruit the reversal of sound building.

row.basis: members care for one another without division
row.note: The commentary makes counsel connect parts; Paul says the body should have no division and its members should have the same care for one another, giving bodily cohesion a reciprocal ethical consequence.

row.basis: חקק ~ ح ق ق; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified
row.note: Isaiah says Zion is engraved on God’s palms and her walls are continually before him; this possible root correspondence extends the commentary’s firm word and bodily-junction imagery to an enduring inscription, without establishing cognacy.

row.basis: reception and giving of rebuke
row.note: The commentary’s mutual counsel in truth resembles the command to reprove one’s neighbor; Arakhin discusses how difficult it is both to give and receive rebuke, making reciprocal correction a demanding practice rather than a simple formula.

row.basis: firm foundation paired with turning from iniquity
row.note: The commentary opposes sound construction to a weak house and corruption; 2 Timothy says God’s firm foundation stands, then pairs its seal with the command to depart from iniquity, joining structural security to ethical conduct.
